NG.name: Igbo
NG.desc: Igbo marriage involves several stages: "Iku Aka" (knocking), "Ije Uche" (family agreement), and "Igba Nkwu" (wine carrying ceremony). The bride carries a cup of palm wine through the crowd to find her groom — one of the most heartwarming moments in African weddings!
NG.dyk: In traditional Igbo culture, the groom must identify his bride from a group of women — all wearing identical outfits! If he picks the wrong one… awkward. 😬

NG.name: Yoruba
NG.desc: Yoruba engagement is a grand affair! The "Introduction" ceremony features the groom's family in matching aso-ebi, prostrating before elders, and presenting a carefully listed dowry. The ceremony is filled with dance, music, and plenty of "spraying" money!
NG.dyk: Yoruba bride price is famously one of the lowest in Nigeria — sometimes just ₦5,000! But the engagement party and aso-ebi can cost millions. The real expense is the party, not the bride price itself. 💃🎉

NG.name: Hausa
NG.desc: In Hausa culture, the groom pays "Sadaki" (Islamic dowry to the bride herself) and "Kayan Lefe" (gifts to the bride's family). The process is guided by Islamic principles of simplicity, though modern practice can be elaborate.
NG.dyk: In Islamic tradition, the Sadaki is actually given to the bride herself — not her family. It's her personal property that even her husband cannot claim. Girl power! 💪

KE.name: Kikuyu
KE.desc: Ruracio involves several visits. The first "Kumenya Mucii" is introductory. The actual ruracio negotiation is spirited — with uncles on both sides doing serious but good-natured haggling. Goats are central!
KE.dyk: During Kikuyu ruracio, the uncles negotiating for the bride's family are legendary for their tough bargaining. They'll test the groom's patience — it's part of proving you're worthy! Some negotiations last 6+ hours. ⏰

KE.name: Luo
KE.desc: Luo marriage negotiations involve "Nyombo" (bride price) traditionally paid in cattle. The groom's family sends trusted emissaries called "Jawuoth" to negotiate. Cattle remain culturally important even when cash is offered.
KE.dyk: In Luo culture, the groom's family brings live cattle to the bride's home. Some modern Luo grooms in Nairobi hire cattle for the day and return them after the ceremony. Resourceful! 😂🐄

GH.name: Akan (Ashanti)
GH.desc: The Akan "Tiri Nsa" (head drink) involves the groom's family presenting schnapps to formally ask for the bride. It's one of the most affordable bride price traditions in Africa — the emphasis is on respect, not money.
GH.dyk: Ashanti bride price is famously affordable! The entire "Tiri Nsa" can cost less than a nice dinner in Accra. The Ashanti say: "We don't sell our daughters — we welcome our sons." ❤️

GH.name: Ewe
GH.desc: Ewe "Tsifo" is also very affordable and respectful. The groom presents modest gifts and drinks. The ceremony emphasizes family unity over financial exchange.
GH.dyk: The Ewe people have one of the most egalitarian marriage systems in Africa. The bride price is intentionally kept low to ensure marriage is accessible to all. 🙌

ZA.name: Zulu
ZA.desc: Lobola is negotiated through an "Umkhongi" (mediator). Traditionally 11 cattle — 10 for the bride and 1 for the mother ("Inkomo Kamama"). Modern Zulu lobola has moved largely to cash but the cow metaphor remains in negotiations.
ZA.dyk: Zulu lobola negotiations still refer to "heads of cattle" even when paying cash! One cow = ~R15,000-R20,000. And yes, having a degree can add 1-2 extra cows to the price. Education literally pays… for the in-laws! 🎓🐄

ZA.name: Xhosa
ZA.desc: Xhosa lobola follows a similar pattern to Zulu. Blankets are culturally significant — the iconic Xhosa blanket is a key gift. Negotiations are formal but infused with ubuntu (humanity).
ZA.dyk: The Xhosa blanket is so culturally important that Nelson Mandela wore one during his most iconic moments. During lobola, presenting the right blankets shows deep cultural respect. 🇿🇦

UG.name: Baganda
UG.desc: The Kwanjula is THE event in Buganda culture. The groom arrives with a huge entourage, introduces himself, and presents gifts. There's a hilarious tradition where the bride is hidden among look-alikes — the groom must find her!
UG.dyk: At a Kwanjula, the groom's entourage must find the real bride among several women dressed identically. If you pick wrong, you pay a fine! Some grooms bring binoculars. Just kidding. Maybe. 🔍😂

TZ.name: Chagga
TZ.desc: The Chagga people from the slopes of Kilimanjaro have a proud marriage tradition. Mahari is paid in cattle or cash, and the ceremony includes traditional banana beer (Mbege) and plenty of celebration.
TZ.dyk: Chagga people live on the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro and brew "Mbege" — a banana beer central to marriage ceremonies. They say: "A man who cannot brew Mbege cannot keep a wife." Brewing skills = husband material!

ET.name: Amhara
ET.desc: Ethiopian Orthodox marriage involves multiple stages: the "Ye Qurban" church blessing, family negotiations, and the "Ye Sir Gabcha" (secret engagement). The groom's family sends emissaries ("Ye Sir Yaze") who present gifts to formally request the bride. Coffee plays a central role — negotiations often happen during elaborate coffee ceremonies.
ET.dyk: In Amhara tradition, the groom must demonstrate character through a series of family visits before any negotiations begin. The family's elders observe the suitor closely — how he eats, how he greets elders, even how he holds his coffee cup. First impressions last a lifetime!

MA.name: Amazigh (Berber)
MA.desc: North African Amazigh marriage follows Islamic principles combined with ancient Berber customs. The "Sadak" (Islamic mahr) is given directly to the bride. Pre-wedding ceremonies span several days: the "Hammam" purification bath, the "Henna night", and the multi-day wedding celebration with traditional Amazigh music and dress.
MA.dyk: In Amazigh tradition, the bride's henna night lasts until dawn — intricate patterns are drawn by elder women who tell the story of the bride's new journey in the designs. The darker the henna, the stronger the love. The groom is not allowed to see the designs until after the wedding!
